extracted.intended_audience: military commanders (General Marmont and subordinate commanders) in the 1809 Napoleonic campaign
extracted.subtask_description: Operational and logistical orders for conducting the 1809 campaign around Gratz/Znaïm, including timelines, river crossings, corps dispositions, siege requirements, communications, reconnaissance, and island/bridge defenses. Targets are corps commanders and engineers executing the Emperor's and major-general's instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dates are of the utmost importance
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Les dates sont de la dernière importance.' — ensure communications and reports show correct and precise dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several letters stress that an incorrect date (e.g., 1st June vs 11th) can produce confusion. Timeliness and correct dating of orders and reports is repeatedly emphasised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain and secure communications with Gratz
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain the communication line to Gratz and operate wherever the enemy is (Marburg, Pétau, everywhere the enemy may be).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit instruction to keep communication open and, if possible, to march on Gratz; orders are both strategic (hold communications) and tactical (move to cut or secure lines). If citadel taken, leave a garrison to maintain communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue and prevent enemy concentration on Gratz
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursue the enemy (e.g., General Chasteler, Giulay) and prevent their movement toward Gratz.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orders instruct following and harrying enemy columns so they cannot mass on Gratz; when practicable, attack to 'culbuter' (crush) opposing corps and force the citadel to surrender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act on general intent; circumstances must guide movements
rubrics_metrics.description: Where distant, directions are 'rather general than positive' and circumstances must decide movements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commands indicate latitude when far from the Commander-in-Chief: obey intent (e.g., hold communications, march on enemy) but adapt to local intelligence and obstacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and surety of movement; go directly to objective
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Ce qui convient à la guerre est de la simplicité et de la sûreté' — when possible, move directly to the objective (e.g., Gratz) rather than detours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Napoleon criticises detours (e.g., marching on Wildon) that cost days; straightforward movements provide better intelligence and operational advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send daily officers/regular reports
rubrics_metrics.description: When large decisions are imminent, send officers daily to bring news and keep the command informed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major-General reproves Marmont for not sending daily news and stresses the need for regular reports so higher command can decide and coordinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be timely and seize opportunities; an hour can decide armies
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Le destin des armées... dépend d'une heure.' — act promptly to follow enemy retirements and attack rearguards; avoid unnecessary delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to move within a day can miss opportunities to engage or cut enemy forces; commanders must press advantage when the enemy retreats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure obedience and effective subordinate command
rubrics_metrics.description: Commanders must be able to make their troops obey; incompetent subordinates (e.g., Montrichard) who compromise operations should be replaced or disciplined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marmont is urged to correct or recommend replacement of officers whose behaviour repeatedly jeopardises operations; failure of subordinates to execute orders may lead to court-martial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain lines of communication toward Vienna
rubrics_metrics.description: The corps' line of communication must be on Vienna; detachments left in rear must join Klagenfurth or Vienna; only specified places keep garrisons (Klagenfurth, Laybach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All rear elements should be organized to preserve the main communication route to Vienna; this governs where to leave garrisons and how to relocate magazines and supplies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redistribute munitions and artillery reserves to strategic depots
rubrics_metrics.description: Send reserve men/munitions (e.g., from Broussier: 'fifteen cent mille cartouches') and artillery companies to Bruck, Neustadt, and thence to Vienna without delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Napoleon orders immediate dispatch of munitions and two companies of the 8th foot artillery to Vienna and instructs making 'great days' marches to expedite delivery; Marmont must instruct and report orders to effect this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave garrison or blocking rear-guard when unable to take fortress
rubrics_metrics.description: If cannot take the castle of Gratz, leave an effective rear-guard to blockade the citadel and instruct the commander not to evacuate until one or two days after main force departs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the citadel cannot be captured without heavy guns, a blocking force should be left to fix the garrison and protect communications; timing of evacuation is explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Siege requires heavy guns, powder, and engineers
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'impossibilité absolue' to take the fort without heavy guns; siege requires large calibre pieces, powder, sappers and engineers, and time for mining and works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marmont requests four pieces of heavy calibre from Laybach and powder; initial siege works started with two good engineers and a company of sappers. Commanders must plan logistical requests early and estimate time needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not desorganize scarce artillery by over-detaching crews
rubrics_metrics.description: When ordered to send artillery companies away, ensure the remainder can still serve available guns; avoid disorganising the little artillery left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marmont objects that sending two foot artillery companies would leave no one to serve his seventeen guns; decisions should weigh crew needs against depot requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reconnaissance and screened detachments to obtain reliable intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Send strong vanguards and reconnaissance elements far (six to seven leagues) to obtain certain news of enemy movements; use parties to observe rivers and key routes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marmont sent strong vanguards six to seven leagues to follow and track enemy; Major-General and Montbrun recommend observing river March and flanks to avoid enemy raids on the rear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post cavalry pickets to mark roads and ensure news arrival
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave cavalry posts to jalonner (mark) the route so news arrives promptly and to secure bridges and key points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Napoleon reproaches Marmont for not leaving posts at bridges; cavalry posts should be left at half-hour/timed intervals; scouts sent in multiple (e.g., three) at staggered intervals reduce mission failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send scouts/engineers in multiple, staggered detachments
rubrics_metrics.description: When sending an officer or engineer on a critical mission, send several at staggered intervals (e.g., three at half-hour distances) to ensure arrival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Napoleon: the Italian engineer took six hours and others never arrived; the rule of war is to send multiple men spaced to avoid single-point failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange corps and lines for river crossing and initial battle formation
rubrics_metrics.description: For the planned Danube operation: three corps in first line (Rivoli left, Oudinot centre, Auerstädt right); second line composition, cuirassiers reserve as third line; specific corps assigned to left/centre/right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ORDRE lists detailed corps dispositions and the order in which they pass the bridges and form lines; each corps must place divisions left/centre/right and keep regimental artillery in battalion intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct coordinated amphibious assault with naval and engineering support
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks include: Captain Baste with armed boats to protect landing and enfilade enemy batteries; Oudinot to embark 1,500 men for Hausl-Grund landing; use bacs and cinquenelle to ferry troops and materiel; pontonniers to construct a bridge in two hours; seize woods and secure riverbank approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed sequence: initial protected landing, placement of 800 men in four bacs to land at enemy battery foot, use of a cinquenelle (haul-line) to shuttle ferries, rapid construction of pontoon bridges, and immediate debouching to clear woods and secure positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use layered bridging: pont d'une pièce, rafts, ponts on pontoons
rubrics_metrics.description: After bacs double the island Alexandre, a 'pont d'une pièce' is to be descended and placed, then rafts and pontoons used to build further bridges allowing artillery and cavalry over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bridging sequence is timed to let the duke of Rivoli and then other corps cross on progressively larger, more permanent bridges; engineers assigned specific bridge tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure islands and flanking batteries with marines/sailors
rubrics_metrics.description: Seize the islands (Rohr-Tsith, Alexandre, etc.), land artillery pieces to form batteries flanking enemy positions, and support them with sailors (e.g., 200 marins) armed with small arms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captain Baste and naval detachments tasked to take islands and deploy small batteries to enfilade enemy positions while protecting army landing and passage operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign clear command and composition of corps and cavalry brigades
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify which divisions and cavalry brigades compose each corps, who commands them, and which units to leave with island/head-of-bridge defence (e.g., Reynier to command island defence with specified battalions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ORDRE articles enumerate divisions, who leaves what battalions in reserve or for bridge-heads, and which cavalry brigades fall under specific corps command—clarity of assignment is critical to coordinated action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralize island/bridge defence under a single commander with authority to move batteries
rubrics_metrics.description: General Reynier to command island; all island batteries and bridge guards under his orders; he may execute changes and reassign pieces where circumstances require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrated command simplifies reallocation of guns and troops during dynamic battle conditions; explicit list of battalions and their location on islands/head-of-bridge is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deploy armed boats and naval craft to observe, harass, and protect river approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Place armed vessels between specific points to harass the enemy, watch for enemy enterprises against the Prater or the right bank, and stop enemy fire-ships; keep other armed boats on the right to protect the descent and our right flank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title V prescribes exact locations for gunboats to both harass and provide early warning, supplementing land-based batteries during river operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve local supplies and seize useful industrial/logistical assets
rubrics_metrics.description: Conserve magazines and manutentions, secure important factories (e.g., tabac factory at Znaïm) to supply the army; evacuate hospitals toward safe points like Bruck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major-General instructs Marmont to conserve supplies and to remove postal letters; taking local manufacturing/stockpiles is a priority when resources are scarce at home base (Vienne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use strong vanguards to harry retreating enemy and capture baggage/prisoners
rubrics_metrics.description: Push forward brigades of reconnaissance and pursue rear-guards to capture wounded, baggage, and horses; objective is to leave a portion of the enemy's train/cavalry in our hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montbrun reports successes when pushing cavalry recon and brigades to catch enemy rear-guards and baggage; such actions degrade enemy capability and yield prisoners and materiel.
